About me

Hi, I’m Makenna Phillips, a Spatial Data Science and Technology and Anthropology student at the University of Oregon. My academic interests include GIS, demographic analysis, urban geography, hazards, accessibility, and community resilience. I am currently a COPES Fellow conducting research through an NSF-funded hazards research hub focused on the Cascadia region.

I am especially interested in projects that connect data visualization with real places and lived histories. This final portfolio uses Jefferson County and Beaumont, Texas, because the region gives a strong example of how racial geography, housing, and economic patterns can be explored through maps.

GEOG 490 Case Study

Jefferson County and Beaumont-Port Arthur, Texas

This portfolio tells a short demographic story about Jefferson County, Texas, with a focus on the Beaumont area. The maps and charts show how race, income, housing, age, and commuting patterns vary across the region.

Main argument

The demographic landscape of Jefferson County is not evenly distributed. Black population concentration, local segregation, lower income areas, and older housing patterns appear clustered in and around Beaumont and Port Arthur, showing how social and economic differences are spatially organized.

Geographic and demographic context

Jefferson County sits in Southeast Texas and includes Beaumont, Port Arthur, and nearby communities. The region has a long history shaped by oil, industry, segregation, and uneven urban development. Because of this history, it is useful to look at demographic patterns spatially rather than only through county-wide averages.

Race, segregation, and neighborhood concentration

The Black population location quotient map shows where Black residents are more concentrated compared with the county as a whole. Higher values appear in parts of northern Beaumont and Port Arthur, while many outer or less urban areas show lower values. The local multigroup segregation map also shows that segregation is not uniform; some neighborhoods have much stronger separation between groups than others.

Housing and income patterns

Housing value and household income both show clear geographic differences. Lower median home values and lower median household incomes appear in several central urban tracts, while higher values are more visible in some outer and less dense areas. These maps suggest that economic inequality is connected to neighborhood location.

Multivariate analysis

The correlation network and PCA results summarize how several demographic and housing variables relate to one another. Variables such as income, college education, rooms, homeownership, race, density, and structure age do not operate separately. Instead, they form connected patterns that help explain broader neighborhood differences.

Commuting and regional comparison

Mean commute times vary across the Beaumont-Port Arthur region. Jefferson County has the shortest average commute time in this comparison, while Liberty, Chambers, and Hardin counties have longer average travel times. This suggests that work access and regional mobility differ across the broader metropolitan area.

Conclusion

Overall, the maps show that Jefferson County’s demographic and economic patterns are deeply geographic. Race, income, home value, age, and commuting are not spread evenly across the region. Instead, they cluster in ways that reflect urban development, historical segregation, and unequal investment. Mapping these patterns makes the story easier to see because it connects demographic data to the specific places where people live.
